chunk_findings.detail:
`truncate` promises in its docstring that "the footer is inside the budget," but the size check that guards each line is:

```python
if used + size + len(footer(len(lines) - i - 1).encode("utf-8")) > max_bytes and kept:
    break
```

Because of the `and kept` conjunct, the check is a no-op for the very first line (`kept` is still empty, so the whole condition is `False`). The first line is therefore always kept as long as it fits `max_bytes` *by itself*, with no accounting for the footer that will be appended. The result is an output that exceeds `--max-bytes`, directly contradicting the "footer is inside the budget" / cap contract.

Concrete input: `truncate("A"*90 + "\n" + "B\n"*6, max_bytes=100)`.

- `body` is 104 bytes, so the early `len(body) <= max_bytes` return does not fire.
- `lines = ["A"*90+"\n", "B\n", ...]` (7 lines).
- `i=0`: `size = 91`, projected total `91 + len(footer(6)) (~47) = 138 > 100`, but `kept` is empty, so it does **not** break; `91 <= 100`, so no hard-cut either, and line 0 is appended, `used = 91`.
- `i=1`: `91 + 2 + footer(...) > 100` and `kept` is non-empty → break.
- `more = 7 - 1 = 6`; return is `"A"*90 + "\n" + footer(6)` ≈ 138 bytes.

So a 100-byte cap yields ~138 bytes of output. The same happens for any body whose first line fits `max_bytes` alone but whose first line plus footer does not (e.g. a body whose first line is ~59,960 bytes with `--max-bytes 60000`), which is exactly the "first line is the bulk of the document" case the size cap is supposed to bound. The `and kept` guard should only apply after the footer headroom has been reserved, or the first line should go through the same `used + size + footer > max_bytes` check.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/export/frame.py truncate() — the first-line budget short-circuit

chunk_findings.detail:
`render_document`'s docstring promises "The full framed document (header + body), capped to `max_bytes` (0 = uncapped)", but the implementation truncates only the body and *then* prepends the frame:

```python
body = render_body(...)
return frame(truncate(body, max_bytes), k.name, __version__, extra)
```

`truncate` receives the body alone and cannot know the header length, so the header (`<!-- ddflow:generated ... -->` + the "Generated by ddflow ..." line, on the order of 130–150 bytes) is added on top of the cap. Concrete input: `render_document(kind, query, max_bytes=200)` returns a string of roughly 350 bytes — longer than the requested cap — and with the default `max_bytes=60000` the output is ~60,140 bytes. Any consumer that relies on `--max-bytes` to bound stdout (a pager/terminal/pipe limit, a fixed-width field) will get more than it asked for, and if the consumer hard-truncates at exactly `max_bytes` it will cut off the very `[truncated: N more; use --since/--limit]` footer the change promises to make explicit. To satisfy the documented contract, the framing overhead has to be reserved before truncating (e.g. pass `max_bytes - len(frame_header)` to `truncate`, or frame first and then cap), so that header + truncated body stay within `max_bytes`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py:render_document

chunk_findings.detail: The guard test derives the changed-file list with `subprocess.run(["git", "diff", "--name-only", "main...HEAD"], ...).stdout.split()` and never checks `returncode`. If the command fails, `stdout` is empty and `out` becomes `[]`, so every `assert hot not in out` passes vacuously. Concrete environment: a shallow CI checkout (`actions/checkout` default `fetch-depth: 1`) or any clone where the `main` ref is not fetched/does not exist locally — `git diff main...HEAD` exits 128, prints nothing to stdout, and the test reports success even if `ddflow/views/markdown.py`, `ddflow/core/model.py`, or `pyproject.toml` were in fact edited. Likewise, when the change under review is sitting in the working tree (uncommitted), `main...HEAD` compares commits only and reports none of the uncommitted edits, again passing without verifying the "touches no hot file" acceptance criterion. In both cases the test's stated guarantee ("no hot file is edited") is not actually enforced, giving false confidence.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_export_core.py::test_no_new_dependency_and_no_hot_files

titles: ddflow/services/export/frame.py truncate() — the first-line budget short-circuit

chunk_findings.detail:
`truncate` can return a string longer than `max_bytes`. The footer is only counted against the budget inside the loop check `if used + size + len(footer(...)) > max_bytes and kept: break`, but that check is short-circuited for the first line because `kept` is empty, and the hard-cut branch (`if used + size > max_bytes`) also compares against `max_bytes` without reserving room for the footer. So a first line whose size is in `(max_bytes - footer_len, max_bytes]` is added whole, and then the footer is appended on top. Concrete: `truncate("a"*93 + "
" + "bbbbbbbb
", 100)` produces `"a"*93 + "
" + "[truncated: 1 more lines; use --since/--limit]
"` = 141 bytes, even though the body (103 bytes) exceeded the cap and the function is documented as "Cut body to at most max_bytes UTF-8 bytes ... The footer is inside the budget." The same gap shows up at the default cap whenever the first rendered line is ~59,954–60,000 bytes, and in the hard-cut path for caps below ~47 (e.g. `truncate("x"*1000, 10)` returns the ~48-byte `"
[truncated: 0 more lines; ...]
"`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py:truncate

chunk_findings.detail: When the body is a single over-long line, the footer reports `0 more lines` although most of the content was dropped. `lines` has one element; the first line is hard-cut and kept, the loop ends, `more = len(lines) - len(kept) = 0`. Concrete: `truncate("x"*200, 100)` returns `"x"*20 + "\n" + "[truncated: 0 more lines; use --since/--limit]\n"`, i.e. the footer asserts nothing is missing after 180 of 200 characters were removed. That contradiction ("a reader (or an agent) never mistakes a cut document for a complete one") is exactly the case the footer exists to prevent; the count is line-based but the cut here is mid-line, and no indication of the partial line is emitted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py:truncate

chunk_findings.detail: `render_document` is documented (and named) as producing "The full framed document (header + body), capped to `max_bytes`", but only the body is capped: `truncate(body, max_bytes)` runs first and `frame(...)` then *prepends* the two header lines (`<!-- ddflow:generated ... -->` ≈ 71 bytes plus `Generated by ddflow from the event log - edit the source, not this file` ≈ 73 bytes, ~146 bytes total) outside the budget. Given `max_bytes=100`, the returned string is ~250 bytes, i.e. the emitted output is ~2.5× the requested cap. Since `--max-bytes` is described in the intent as the stdout size cap (not a body-only cap), any caller that uses this flag to bound output size (notification limits, chunked writes) gets a document that violates the contract. Concrete: `render_document("tasks", q, max_bytes=100)` returns > 200 bytes even though the body was cut at 100. If the cap is meant to bound emitted bytes, the header (and any frame trailer) length must be subtracted from `max_bytes` before calling `truncate`, or the returned header+body must be re-checked.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py:render_document

chunk_findings.detail: `_discovered[0] = True` is set *before* the import loop, so a failure while importing any `kind_*.py` leaves the registry permanently "discovered" in a partial state. Concretely, with two modules `kind_a.py` and `kind_b.py` that both `register(DocKind(name="a", ...))`, the first `names()`/`get()` call raises the `ValueError("export kind 'a' is already registered")` from `kind_b`'s import; a second call in the same process (e.g. a subsequent test, or any retry) now returns immediately from `discover()` and silently yields only the kinds registered before the failure (`["a"]`), never re-raising the error. Setting the guard only after the loop completes (or clearing it in an `except`/`finally` on failure) would make the failure deterministic instead of order-dependent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py:discover

chunk_findings.detail: `git diff --name-only main...HEAD` only diffs *committed* trees (the three-dot form ignores the working tree and index). So the test does not verify what it claims: the acceptance criterion is "views/markdown.py is NOT edited", but a developer who edits `ddflow/views/markdown.py` (or `ddflow/core/model.py`, or adds a dependency line to `pyproject.toml`) and runs the suite before committing gets `out` that does not contain the hot file, and all three assertions pass. Example: `echo x >> ddflow/views/markdown.py; pytest tests/test_export_core.py::test_no_new_dependency_and_no_hot_files` passes while the hot file is modified. The same command also silently degenerates to an empty `out` whenever the base ref is unavailable (e.g. `actions/checkout` default `fetch-depth: 1`, where no local `main` exists, or a repo whose default branch is `master`): `subprocess.run` has no `check=True`, so the `fatal: ...` error goes to stderr, `stdout` is `""`, `out == []`, and every `assert hot not in out` trivially holds. In both cases the acceptance test can never fail on a real violation.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_export_core.py:255 (test_no_new_dependency_and_no_hot_files)

chunk_findings.detail:
In the "not even one whole line fits" branch, the byte budget and the actual output use footers of different lengths. `room = max_bytes - size(footer(n - 1)) - 1` sizes the cut line against `footer(n - 1)`, but the returned string appends `footer(n)` (line 138). Whenever `n` and `n - 1` have different digit counts — i.e. `n` is 10, 100, 1000, … — `footer(n)` is one byte longer than the value that was budgeted, so the result exceeds `max_bytes` by exactly one byte, violating the function's documented guarantee ("the result never exceeds max_bytes", line 120) and the acceptance requirement of a working `--max-bytes` cap.

Concrete case: `truncate(body, 200)` where `body` is 10 lines and its first line is ≥154 bytes. The `best` loop leaves `best == 0` (since `first_line + footer(9) > 200`), `shown` is empty, so line 136 computes `room = 200 - len(footer(9)) - 1 = 200 - 47 - 1 = 152`. The cut line is 152 bytes, and the return at line 138 is `152 + 1 (newline) + len(footer(10)) = 152 + 1 + 48 = 201` bytes — one over the cap, because `footer(10)` is one character longer than the `footer(9)` used to compute `room`. Fixing it requires budgeting with `footer(n)` (the footer actually emitted), not `footer(n - 1)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py:136-138 (`truncate`, mid-line branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring states "``max_bytes`` bounds the WHOLE document", but the floor of `1` means the body budget is never allowed to be smaller than the header reservation. When the requested cap is less than or equal to the header length, the output deliberately overshoots the cap instead of bounding it. Concretely, `render_document(kind, query, ..., max_bytes=50)`: the header `<!-- ddflow:generated doc=… v=… body-sha256=… -->` plus the "Generated by ddflow…" line is >100 bytes, so `overhead > 50`, `max_bytes` becomes `max(50 - overhead, 1) == 1`, and the returned document is `frame(truncate(body, 1), …)`, i.e. the full header (~100+ bytes) plus at least one body byte — strictly larger than the 50 that was requested. Any `--max-bytes` value at or below the header size therefore violates the documented cap; the only reason this is not caught by the acceptance tests is that they use the default 60,000 against a small body.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py `render_document` (the `max(max_bytes - overhead, 1)` reservation)

chunk_findings.detail:
`truncate`'s docstring promises the result "never exceeds max_bytes", but the mid-line cut branch can return `max_bytes + 1` bytes. The `room` computation reserves `footer(n-1)` while the returned string uses `footer(n)`:

```python
room = max_bytes - size(footer(n - 1)) - 1
cut = lines[0].encode("utf-8")[: max(room, 0)].decode("utf-8", "ignore")
return cut.rstrip("\n") + "\n" + footer(n)
```

`footer(k)` is `47 + len(str(k))` bytes, so `footer(n)` is exactly 1 byte larger than `footer(n-1)` when `n` is a power of ten (10, 100, 1000, …). When that branch is entered and the length of the count crosses that boundary, the emitted line is `max_bytes + 1` bytes.

Reproduction: a 10-line body where every line is `"a"*100 + "\n"` (each line 101 bytes, `n = 10`), with `max_bytes = 148`. The `k=1` feasibility test is `101 + footer(9)` = `101 + 48` = `149 > 148`, so `best` stays 0 and the cut branch runs. `room = 148 - 48 - 1 = 99`, so `cut = "a"*99`, and the return value is `"a"*99 + "\n" + footer(10)` = `100 + 49` = `149` bytes, i.e. 1 byte over the requested cap. The same off-by-one occurs at any power-of-ten line count (100, 1000, …). Impact is a 1-byte budget overrun in a narrow case, but it falsifies the stated invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py: truncate (partial-first-line branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `load`'s own docstring promises "never returns an empty Query for a broken log", and the module's rationale is that "a changelog that silently says 'nothing happened' is worse than none". But the only guard is `(root / ".ddflow" / "events").is_dir()`. When the directory exists and the log content is unusable, `EventLog.read_all()` skips the unparseable lines (this file depends on that behaviour — it carries `log.skipped_lines` into the `Query` precisely because unreadable lines are dropped rather than raised) and returns `[]`, so `load` returns `Query(state=<empty>, events=[], skipped_lines=N)` instead of raising `ExportError(EXIT_UNAVAILABLE)`. Concrete input: an events file under `.ddflow/events` that was overwritten/truncated to a single fragment such as `{"ts": "2024-05-0` (no newline) → every line is skipped, `events == []`, and the export exits 0 with an empty document rather than failing with exit 2. The information needed to refuse (`log.skipped_lines > 0` with zero successfully parsed events) is available at the call site but never checked.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py:load

chunk_findings.detail: `since` filtering is a raw string comparison (`e.ts >= since`), so it is only chronological when the caller's string is a literal prefix of the stored `ts`; otherwise lexicographic ordering disagrees with time ordering. Example: events are written with Python's default UTC representation, so the event exactly at the cutoff has `ts == "2024-05-01T12:00:00+00:00"`; a caller passing the equally common `--since 2024-05-01T12:00:00Z` compares `'+' (0x2B) < 'Z' (0x5A)` and the boundary event is dropped, even though `>=` is supposed to include it. With a non-UTC offset the comparison is wrong away from the boundary too: `ts == "2024-05-01T10:00:00+02:00"` (08:00Z) is *kept* for `--since 2024-05-01T09:00:00Z` because `'1' > '0'` in the hour field, so events that happened before the cutoff are included. Parsing `ts`/`since` as datetimes (or normalising both to one canonical form) would be required for correct filtering.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py:events_of

chunk_findings.detail: The function documents "capped to `max_bytes`" and its own comment claims "`max_bytes` bounds the WHOLE document", but the clamp to a floor of 1 does not bound anything once `max_bytes` is at or below the fixed frame overhead. `overhead = len(frame("", ...))` is the length of the header/"Generated by…" block (roughly 140‑150 bytes for a normal kind/version), and it cannot be reduced. With `max_bytes=10` the reservation yields `max(10 - 145, 1) == 1`, so `truncate(body, 1)` returns at least 1 byte and `frame(...)` then prepends the ~145‑byte header unconditionally. The returned document is therefore ~146 bytes long for a request of 10 — i.e. the emitted stdout can exceed the requested `--max-bytes` by the entire header length whenever a caller passes a value smaller than the header. Concretely, `render_document(kind, query, max_bytes=10)` (or 50, or 100) returns a string longer than `max_bytes`, contradicting both the docstring and the "bounds the WHOLE document" comment. The correct handling would be to raise/refuse when `max_bytes <= overhead`, or to include the overflow explicitly, rather than silently producing a document larger than the cap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py `render_document` (`max_bytes = max(max_bytes - overhead, 1)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The header contract says `body-sha256=<12 hex>`, but no test in this file pins that. `test_golden_document_has_header_and_digest` builds its expected header with `digest = frame.body_digest(GOLDEN_BODY)` and then asserts `doc == "... body-sha256={digest} ..."`, i.e. the expected value is produced by the same function under test. The same circularity appears in `test_header_extra_attrs_round_trip` (`"body-sha256=" + frame.body_digest("x\n")`). Nothing anywhere asserts the digest is 12 hex characters, that it is hex at all, or that it equals a known hash of a known input (`head.digest == digest` is also just `body_digest == body_digest` because `frame.split` and `frame.frame` share the helper). Concrete failure that should be caught but is not: change `body_digest` to return `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` (64 chars, or `[:8]`, or `sha1`). Every assertion is recomputed from the new value, so the whole suite still passes while the emitted header violates the documented `body-sha256=<12 hex>` format and any downstream parser/deduplicator that assumes the fixed length breaks.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_export_core.py: test_golden_document_has_header_and_digest

chunk_findings.detail: The spec's acceptance footer is the literal `[truncated: N more; use --since/--limit]`, but the implementation emits a different string: `footer()` returns `f"[truncated: {n} more lines; use --since/--limit]\n"` (and the module docstring repeats "N more lines"). Given a fixture log whose rendered body exceeds `--max-bytes`, the emitted stdout/stdin text is e.g. `[truncated: 5 more lines; use --since/--limit]` where the required text is `[truncated: 5 more; use --since/--limit]`. Because the acceptance criterion is "golden files from a small fixture log" and "the truncation footer is explicit," an exact-bytes golden comparison fails on every truncated document (the extra word "lines"). Either the golden fixtures must be regenerated against this wording, or the footer must be changed to match the specified format.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py:118 (truncate / footer)

chunk_findings.detail: `_cutoff` promises "An unparseable `since` is refused, never ignored", but the short-string branch returns a comparator without ever validating the input. Any `since` whose length is ≤ `_DATE_LEN` (10) bypasses `_parse_ts` entirely and is used as a raw `ts[:len(since)] >= since` prefix compare. So a garbage value such as `--since garbage` (len 7) or a typo like `--since 2026-1O-01` (capital O, len 10) is accepted silently: for `"2026-10".… >= "garbage"` the comparison is False for every event, so `events_of` returns an empty list and the caller renders a blank document with no `ExportError`. This is exactly the outcome the module says it must avoid ("a changelog that silently says 'nothing happened' is worse than none"), and it contradicts the docstring right above the return. The full-timestamp branch (len > 10) correctly raises `ExportError(..., EXIT_REFUSED)`, so the validation is only missing on the `<= _DATE_LEN` path; a valid check would parse/validate the date prefix there too.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py `_cutoff` (`if len(since) <= _DATE_LEN:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
The minimum-cap guard is applied unconditionally, but the bytes it reserves (`MIN_BODY_BYTES = 80`, described as "a truncation footer plus a little text") are only ever needed when the body is actually truncated — the `[truncated: N more; ...]` footer is emitted by `truncate()` only when it cuts the body. As written, a cap that is large enough for the document actually produced is still refused (exit 3).

Concrete case: take a kind whose `data`/template produce a 5-byte body and whose header (with body-sha256 and `extra`) frames to ~69 bytes, so the whole document is ~74 bytes. Calling `render_document(kind, query, max_bytes=120)` raises `ExportError(..., EXIT_REFUSED)` because `120 < 69 + 80 = 149`, even though the framed output (74 bytes) is well inside the requested 120. The same happens for any `--max-bytes` in `[overhead + body, overhead + 80)`: the command fails for a cap that in fact bounds the output. The guard should only fire when truncation is actually required (i.e. `overhead + len(body.encode("utf-8")) > max_bytes`), or reserve `overhead + len(footer)` rather than a fixed 80.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py `render_document` (the `if max_bytes < overhead + MIN_BODY_BYTES` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: `_cutoff` dispatches on string length (`len(since) <= _DATE_LEN`), and only the "long" branch attempts parsing and can raise `ExportError(..., EXIT_REFUSED)`. Any malformed `since` of 10 or fewer characters is silently turned into a raw prefix comparison `ts[:len(since)] >= since` instead of being refused, contradicting the function's own docstring ("An unparseable `since` is refused, never ignored") and the module's stated goal that a filter error must never yield a clean-looking empty document. Concrete case: `--since 2026-13-01` (invalid month, exactly `_DATE_LEN = 10` chars) is not parsed; the predicate becomes `ts[:10] >= "2026-13-01"`, and since every real ISO date prefix is at most `"2026-12-31"`, the comparison is `False` for every event. The caller then renders an empty export and exits 0 — exactly the "silently says nothing happened" failure the file explicitly warns against — rather than exiting `EXIT_REFUSED` (3). The same holds for obvious typos such as `--since abc` or `--since yesterday`, all ≤ 10 chars, which likewise match nothing and suppress no error. The short branch is only correct for genuinely valid zero-padded date prefixes (`2026`, `2026-10`, `2026-10-01`); it cannot distinguish those from garbage, so the refusal guarantee is unmet for the whole short-input class.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py:166 (`_cutoff`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring promises the result "never exceeds max_bytes (unless the footer alone does, which no sane cap allows)", but the empty-prefix branch still emits a separator newline that is not budgeted for when `max_bytes` equals the footer size. Concretely, `truncate("x" * 100 + "
", 41)`: the body (101 bytes) exceeds the cap, `n = 1`, the loop leaves `best = 0` (101 + 41 > 41), so `room = 41 - size(footer(1)) - 1 = 41 - 41 - 1 = -1`, clamped to 0, `cut = ""`, and the function returns `"
" + "[truncated: 1 more; use --since/--limit]
"` = 42 bytes. So the output exceeds the cap by one byte as soon as `max_bytes <= size(footer)`, i.e. the documented carve-out ("unless the footer alone does [not fit]") is itself off by one — the `- 1` accounting for the join newline is only applied when `room >= 0`, and when `room < 0` it clamps to 0 yet still prepends the `"
"`. Any caller that passes a small `--max-bytes` (e.g. a token-budgeted render) gets output larger than the requested cap with no indication that the cap was unattainable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/frame.py `truncate` (empty-prefix branch, line ~110-113)

chunk_findings.detail: `render`'s docstring promises that a *sandbox violation* is turned into `ExportError` (exit 2, "could not run"), and the inline comment at line 289 explicitly claims `SecurityError` is covered by `except jinja2.TemplateError`. It is not: in Jinja2, `jinja2.sandbox.SecurityError` derives directly from `Exception`, **not** from `jinja2.TemplateError`. The sandbox denies an `_`-prefixed attribute by returning `self.undefined(msg, name=attribute, exc=SecurityError)` (i.e. a `StrictUndefined` whose failure exception is `SecurityError`); converting that undefined to text raises `SecurityError` at render time. Concrete input: a project override `.ddflow/templates/export/<kind>.md.j2` containing `{{ ''.__class__.__mro__ }}` (or any `class`/`mro`/`globals` escape). `render` → `_environment().from_string(...).render(...)` raises `jinja2.sandbox.SecurityError`, which matches neither `jinja2.TemplateSyntaxError`, nor `jinja2.TemplateError`, nor the `(TimeoutError, RecursionError, OverflowError, TypeError, ValueError, ArithmeticError)` tuple, so it escapes `render`, `render_body` and `render_document` as a raw `SecurityError` instead of the documented `ExportError`. Any caller written against that contract (catching `ExportError` to print the "could not run" message and return exit code 2) instead sees an unhandled exception/traceback, and in the server-worker case the docstring itself says the sandbox is the only guard for a template that "came with a cloned repository", so this path becomes an uncaught 500 rather than a clean exit-2 refusal. Fix: add `jinja2.SecurityError` (e.g. `except (jinja2.TemplateError, jinja2.SecurityError)`) or catch `Exception` for the sandbox/lookup group.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/export/registry.py:289 (the `except jinja2.TemplateError` clause, and the docstring at line 275)

chunk_findings.detail:
`Header.line()` serialises `extra` values verbatim (`f" {k}={v}"`), but `_HEADER_RE` only accepts keys matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` and values matching `\S+`. Any extra whose value contains a space, whose value is empty, or whose key contains a character outside that class (e.g. a dot) produces a header that the module's own parser cannot read. Concretely, `frame("x\n", "roadmap", "0.1.9", {"title": "Q4 Plan"})` emits
`<!-- ddflow:generated doc=roadmap v=0.1.9 body-sha256=... title=Q4 Plan -->`.
`split()` then returns `(None, text)` (the ` extra` group matches ` title=Q4` but the required ` -->` cannot follow ` Plan`), and `hand_edited()` returns `None` for a file ddflow itself just wrote. Since `--check`/the writer use `None` to mean "an unmarked file is not ours", hand-edit protection silently fails open (treated as foreign, not as "edited") for any kind that records a human-readable extra such as a template name/title. The digest itself is fine; the writer/parser contract is not.

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring guarantees the result never exceeds `max_bytes` "unless the footer alone does", but the empty-`shown` branch always appends an unconditional `"
"` on top of `footer(n)`, so the cap is exceeded by one byte even when the footer *does* fit. Example: `truncate("a"*100 + "
" + "b
"*9, 42)`. Here `n = 10`, the largest fitting prefix is 0 (line 1 alone is 101 bytes > 42), so `room = 42 - len(footer(10)) - 1 = 42 - 42 - 1 = -1`, `max(room, 0)` makes `cut == ""`, and the function returns `"" + "
" + footer(10)` = 43 bytes, exceeding the requested 42 even though the footer alone is exactly 42. Any `max_bytes < len(footer(n)) + 1` shares this off-by-one, so the "footer inside the budget" property does not hold at the boundary. (The broader case where the footer alone already exceeds the cap is disclaimed in the docstring; this one is not.)

chunk_findings.detail: `events_of`'s contract, stated in its own docstring, is that "Events whose `ts` cannot be read are left out of a `since`-filtered result". The full-timestamp branch honours this (`at_or_after` returns `False` on `ValueError`), but the bare-date branch (the common `--since 2026-10-01` case) does no parsing at all — it compares the first `len(since)` characters lexicographically. With `since="2026-10-01"` and an event whose `ts` is unparseable but lexicographically high, e.g. `ts="unknown"` / `ts="2026-10-05-broken"`, `"unknown"[:10] >= "2026-10-01"` evaluates to `True` (`'u' > '2'`), so the event is *included* in the result even though its timestamp demonstrably cannot be shown to be in range. The same event is excluded when `since` is given as a full timestamp (`_parse_ts` raises, `at_or_after` returns `False`), so the two accepted forms of `--since` disagree about the very same event. The code explicitly anticipates unreadable `ts` values in the timestamp branch, so this is not a hypothetical input class; the fix is to validate/parse `ts` in the date branch too (e.g. skip a `ts` whose date prefix is not itself a valid ISO date) rather than trusting a raw string slice.

chunk_findings.detail: In `render()`, the call `ctx = plain(dict(data))` is executed *before* the `try:` that converts rendering failures into `ExportError`. `plain()` is recursive over the kind's return value, and a self-referential structure is built entirely out of values that pass the `_PLAIN`/`Mapping`/`list` type checks, so it recurses until Python raises `RecursionError`. Because that happens outside the `try`, the `except (... RecursionError ...)` clause never sees it, and the documented contract ("Any failure … raises ExportError (exit 2, could not run)"; "A kind returning anything else is a bug in the kind and is reported as one") is broken. Concrete input: a kind whose `data()` returns `d = {}; d["self"] = d` — `render()` raises a bare `RecursionError` (unhandled traceback / non-2 exit) instead of an `ExportError`. The same applies to any nesting deeper than the interpreter recursion limit. Catching/moving `plain()` inside the `try` (or guarding against cycles) fixes it.

chunk_findings.detail: `render`'s docstring promises that *any* failure inside template rendering (outside syntax/undefined) raises `ExportError` (exit 2, could not run), and the acceptance requires template failures to exit 2 without partial output. But the except tuple only covers a hand-picked subset of exception types. Jinja does not wrap exceptions raised by method/filter calls, so a template that calls an ordinary sandbox-safe method which raises `LookupError` (of which `IndexError`/`KeyError` are subclasses) escapes uncaught. Concrete input: a project override template containing `{{ [].pop() }}` (or `{{ {}.popitem() }}`). `[].pop()` is sandbox-safe (`is_internal_attribute` is False for `"pop"`), raises `IndexError`, which is not a `jinja2.TemplateError` and is not in the tuple above, so it propagates out of `render`/`render_body`/`render_document` as a raw `IndexError` rather than `ExportError`. The same holds for `{{ "x".encode("no-such-codec") }}` (`LookupError`). Result: the documented "template error ⇒ exit 2, nothing written" contract is violated for these templates (unhandled exception / wrong exit status), even though the syntax- and undefined-variable paths the acceptance tests happen to exercise are covered.

chunk_findings.detail:
`truncate` promises "at most `max_bytes` UTF-8 bytes", but when the footer alone does not fit it returns the bare footer, which is larger than the cap. The footer is 41 bytes (`len("[truncated: N more; use --since/--limit]
")`). So for any `max_bytes` in `[1, 40]`, `room = max_bytes - size(footer(n)) - 1` is `<= 0` and the function returns the 41-byte footer, exceeding the requested cap. Concrete: `truncate("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
", 10)` returns `[truncated: 1 more; use --since/--limit]
` (41 bytes) instead of at most 10. Since `max_bytes` is a user-supplied CLI value (`--max-bytes`), a caller relying on the cap (e.g., piping stdout into a bounded buffer) receives more bytes than allowed. (This makes the code comment "unless the footer alone does, which no sane cap allows" the only guarantee the cap has here, i.e. the cap is not actually enforced for small values.)

chunk_findings.detail: The change states as an acceptance criterion that "a template that tries attribute access to reach os/subprocess/file reading (e.g. a class/mro/globals escape) is refused by the sandbox", but the code relies entirely on bare `jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment` and adds no defense against `str.format` / `str.format_map`. The sandbox only intercepts attribute lookup that goes through Jinja (`environment.getattr`, the post-check in the `|attr` filter), i.e. names beginning with `_` or internal-function attributes. The `format` method itself is a normal, "safe" attribute, and the dangerous lookups happen inside CPython's `str.format` machinery, not through Jinja, so they are never checked. A user template taken from a cloned repository therefore escapes: `{{ "{0.__class__.__base__.__subclasses__}".format(0) }}` renders the bound `__subclasses__` method of `object` (proving `__class__`/`__mro__`/`__subclasses__` are reachable), then `{% set cs = ("{0.__class__.__base__.__subclasses__}".format(0))() %}` yields the full subclass list, and `{{ "{0.__init__.__globals__[os]}".format(cs[N]) }}` returns the `os` module from a subclass's `__init__.__globals__` (the `format` spec `[os]` indexes that dict by the literal key `"os"`), reaching `os.popen(...)`/files. Neither `is_safe_attribute` nor any wrapper rejecting `format`/`format_map` is installed, so the acceptance test only passes if it uses the naive underscore form (`{{ ''.__class__ }}`) and never the `format` form.

chunk_findings.detail:
`Header.line()` carefully validates every `extra` attribute against the exact grammar `_HEADER_RE` can parse back (its inline comment says this exists so ddflow never "write[s] a header ddflow itself fails to parse, and hand-edit protection would silently see 'not ours'"), but it never validates `self.doc` or `self.version` — the two fields the regex is strictest about (`doc` is `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`, and the ` v=` / ` body-sha256=` separators must be single spaces). Given `frame("<body>", doc="my doc", version="1.0")`, line returns:

    <!-- ddflow:generated doc=my doc v=1.0 body-sha256=<12hex> -->

Then `split()` runs `_HEADER_RE.match(first)`; the space in `doc=my doc` makes the pattern fail, so it returns `(None, text)`, and `hand_edited()` returns `None` ("not ours") instead of comparing the digest. The file ddflow just wrote is invisible to its own hand-edit/`--check` protection, which is precisely the silent failure the `extra` guard was written to prevent. Any caller that supplies a kind name outside `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+` (or a version containing a space) loses the protection with no error at write time; `frame`/`Header` should either reject such values or derive a validated doc/version.

chunk_findings.detail: `datetime.UTC` was only added in Python 3.11 (`datetime.UTC` is an alias for `datetime.timezone.utc`, introduced in bpo-45379/3.11). On Python 3.10 and earlier this module-level import raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'UTC' from 'datetime'`, so *every* export command fails at import time, not just a `--since` path. The rest of the file is deliberately written for older `datetime` semantics — `_parse_ts` does `text.strip().replace("Z", "+00:00")` precisely because `datetime.fromisoformat` did not accept a trailing `Z` before 3.11 — so the surrounding code is targeting < 3.11 while this import is 3.11-only. Concrete failure: run the export on a Python 3.10 interpreter (the one the `Z`-rewrite implies is supported) with any valid log; `import ddflow.services.export.query` dies before `load()` or `events_of()` is ever reached. The fix is `from datetime import datetime, timezone` and `t.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify the acceptance criterion "a template syntax or undefined-variable error exits 2 and writes nothing", but the `assert not out.exists()` can never fail: `out = tmp_path / "TOY.md"` is never passed to anything, and `registry.render_document(...)` is used everywhere in this file purely for its returned string (e.g. `assert doc == ...` in `test_golden_document_has_header_and_digest`, `assert ... == full` in `test_small_cap_that_the_document_fits_in_is_not_refused`). No code path under test opens or creates `out`, so even an implementation that emitted a partial document/file on a template error would pass this test. Concretely: replace the body of the loop with `registry.render_document(...)` returning a partial string and still writing TOY.md, and this test still passes; the required "writes nothing" behavior is untested here (and no other test in the diff covers it).
